title: Kandu's Nine Hundred Years
hookLine: a sage hurries to his evening prayer, nine centuries late
carry: sandhya: prayer at the turning of the day
tomorrow: the worst age of the world is the best one? who says that?

lines: A SAGE JUMPS UP AT SUNSET.
cards: The phone says nine. You look again and it says one in the morning, and nothing in between felt like four hours. The Vishnu Purana has a sage this happens to, on a much bigger scale.

His name is Kandu. One evening he jumps up in a hurry: the sun is going down, and it's time for his evening prayers by the river. The woman he lives with, Pramlocha, watches him go and stops him with one question.

teach.b: Here's how he got there. Kandu was a sage of great tapas, the heat of hard practice, living by the river Gomati.

Indra, king of the gods, was uneasy at that much power, so he sent Pramlocha, a dancer of heaven, to break Kandu's concentration. It worked. The two of them went to live in a lovely valley, and the days were sweet.
Now and then she asked to go back to heaven, and each time he asked her to stay a little longer. Then that evening.

He's hurrying off to his evening rite, and she tells him the truth: by her count, more than nine hundred years have gone by. He's shaken, and his sharpest words are for himself: all that practice, spent.
He sends her away and goes off to worship Vishnu, back to the practice he had left. Now notice what woke him: the evening prayer.
Its name is sandhya, the joining, the moment one part of the day turns into the next. Traditional Hindu practice keeps prayer at those joints, dawn and dusk above all.
Many who keep the old rite say the Gayatri there, and many homes still light a lamp at sunset.
Many teachers read Kandu's story as a picture of life without those joints: nothing wicked, just one sweet evening that never turned. The sandhya is the tradition's answer.

teach.h: STOP WHERE THE DAY TURNS. REMEMBER GOD.
teach.b: Stop where the day turns, and remember God.

how: Many Hindus pray at the joints of the day: those who keep sandhyavandana say the Gayatri at dawn and dusk, and many homes light a lamp at sunset. The Vishnu Purana tells Kandu's story in its first book.

o: a law book of rules for kings and priests
a single hymn to the sun said at dusk
a Purana of stories centered on Vishnu

games.q: who did what in Kandu's story — tap the pairs.
p: a sage who lost count of the years
sent by Indra to break his concentration

s: Kandu's story says enjoying life is sinful
nothing in it is wicked; the trouble is that he stopped counting.
Kandu thought only one day had passed
he jumps up for evening prayers; Pramlocha tells him it's been centuries.
sandhya is a prayer only priests keep, inside temples
many homes keep it: the Gayatri at dawn and dusk, a lamp lit at sunset.

games.q: your cousin asks why nani stops everything at sunset to light a lamp, even in the middle of a party. by Kandu's story, what's the reason?
o: it's an old superstition about the dark.
sunset is a sandhya, where the day turns; stopping there to remember God keeps the days from blurring together.
it's mostly for show when guests are over.
games.why: Kandu was hurrying to his evening sandhya when he learned nine centuries were gone. the tradition keeps prayer at the day's turning points so evenings don't run together.

practice: Whatever time it is, treat this as a turning of the day. If you pray, light a lamp or face the light, and say a name of God, or the Gayatri if you know it, slowly.
If you don't pray, say out loud what part of the day this is, then sit and notice the turning: the light, the sounds, your own breath. That's a small sandhya, a stop at the joint.

wordCard.voice: The Vishnu Purana. Today's story from it: Kandu, whose evening prayer woke him nine centuries late.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the joining, twilight, and the prayer kept there. Kandu was hurrying to his when he learned the truth.

carryVoice: Your line: sandhya, prayer at the turning of the day. Kandu's evening never turned; yours can. See you tomorrow.
